prompt.context: Our client is a major airline with flights to and from the United States. The CEO has hired Seabury Group to evaluate a promotional campaign for one of its routes, both in terms of the economics and risks involved. The promotion aims to offer full fare passengers a complimentary ticket for one child (under 14) on the same flight.
prompt.question: Should the airline implement this promotion? Evaluate the economics and risks involved.

clarifying_info.q: How many seats does the client offer and how many are sold?
clarifying_info.a: The client offers 1,500,000 seats per year, of which 1,000,000 are usually sold (66% load factor).

clarifying_info.q: What ticket types and prices does the client offer?
clarifying_info.a: Only two price points: Full fare at $300 one way and Discount fare at $100 one way. Discount fare is sold at least 3 weeks in advance.

clarifying_info.q: What is the share of discount vs. full-fare passengers?
clarifying_info.a: 40% of customers travel with discount tickets (400,000 discount, 600,000 full fare).

clarifying_info.q: How are passengers segmented by business vs. leisure?
clarifying_info.a: Out of 1,000,000 passengers: 500,000 are business travelers (100,000 on discount, 400,000 on full fare) and 500,000 are leisure travelers (300,000 on discount, 200,000 on full fare).

clarifying_info.q: What is the variable (marginal) cost per passenger?
clarifying_info.a: The variable cost is $10 per passenger (luggage handling is outsourced and thus variable).

clarifying_info.q: What percentage of passengers would bring children under this promotion?
clarifying_info.a: Of business travelers (full fare), 10% would bring children. Of leisure passengers (full fare), 50% have children and 50% of those are currently traveling with children already.

clarifying_info.q: Are there new customers attracted by the promotion?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, marketing research shows 150,000 new customers attracted by the campaign (each coming with one child, so 300,000 new passengers total).

clarifying_info.q: Will the promotion affect business passenger retention?
clarifying_info.a: Research shows 50,000 business passengers will stop flying with the client due to the increase in children on board.

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost to run the promotion?
clarifying_info.a: The promotion will cost $3,000,000 per year.

framework: Revenue impact: Identify current revenue baseline (price x volume by fare type), then model incremental revenue from new customers attracted by the promotion
Cost impact: Separate fixed costs (aircraft leasing, crew, maintenance, airport staff) from variable/marginal costs (meals, ticketing, outsourced luggage handling) per passenger

Contribution margin analysis: Calculate lost contribution margin from existing passengers who convert to free travel, plus cost of serving new free (child) passengers, plus gain from new paying passengers

Customer segmentation: Break passengers into business vs. leisure and full fare vs. discount; apply promotion economics only to full fare since $300 full fare + free child still exceeds 2x $100 discount
Risk assessment: Business passenger dissatisfaction (children on board), competitive response / price war, consumer habituation to promotion, regulatory/legal considerations
Mitigation options: Separate boarding lines, dedicated check-in, seating children in rear cabin
Net margin conclusion: Sum all incremental contribution margin effects minus promotion overhead cost; compare to zero to decide yes/no

questions.prompt: Calculate the current annual revenue baseline before the promotion.
questions.guidance: Multiply each fare type by its passenger volume. Discount: 400,000 x $100 = $40M. Full fare: 600,000 x $300 = $180M. Total = $220M.

math.setup: Revenue = (discount passengers x discount fare) + (full-fare passengers x full fare)

questions.prompt: Which passenger group should the promotion economics focus on, and why?
questions.guidance: Focus on full-fare passengers only. A full-fare ticket ($300) plus a free child ticket is still more expensive than buying two discount tickets ($200 total), so there is no rational incentive for discount passengers to shift behavior. The case explicitly instructs the interviewee to focus on full-fare passengers.

questions.prompt: Map out the demand changes under the promotion and verify capacity is not breached.
questions.guidance: Three effects on the full-fare base (600,000 passengers): (1) Lost paying children — current full-fare leisure passengers with children who are already paying: 200,000 leisure full-fare x 50% have children x 50% currently traveling with children = 50,000 children who will now fly free instead of paying. (2) New free children from leisure full-fare passengers who have children but are not currently bringing them: 200,000 x 50% x 50% = 50,000 new free passengers. (3) New free children from business full-fare passengers: 400,000 x 10% = 40,000 new free passengers. (4) New paying customers attracted by promotion: 150,000 paying + 150,000 free children = 300,000. Total demand: 1,000,000 + 50,000 + 40,000 + 300,000 = 1,390,000 < 1,500,000 capacity. No capacity constraint.

math.setup: Total passengers = existing + new free leisure children + new free business children + new paying customers + their children
steps: New free leisure children (existing parents, non-traveling kids): 200,000 x 50% x 50% = 50,000
New paying customers + free children: 150,000 x 2 = 300,000

questions.prompt: Calculate the net incremental contribution margin from the promotion before accounting for business passenger churn and promotion cost.
questions.guidance: Three components: (A) Lost contribution from 50,000 existing full-fare paying children now flying free: 50,000 x ($300 - $10) = $14,500,000 loss. (B) Additional marginal cost for all new free passengers (who generate no revenue): (50,000 + 40,000 + 150,000) x $10 = $2,400,000 cost. (C) Additional contribution from 150,000 new paying customers: 150,000 x ($300 - $10) = $43,500,000 gain. Net = $43,500,000 - $14,500,000 - $2,400,000 = $26,600,000.

math.setup: Net margin = revenue gain from new payers - lost CM from converted free children - marginal cost of all new free passengers
steps: Lost CM from 50,000 existing paying children now free: 50,000 x ($300 - $10) = $14,500,000
CM gain from 150,000 new paying customers: 150,000 x ($300 - $10) = $43,500,000

questions.prompt: Adjust for business passenger churn: 50,000 business passengers leave due to children on board.
questions.guidance: 50,000 business full-fare passengers who defect each represent lost contribution of ($300 - $10) = $290. Total lost CM = $14,500,000. Revised net margin = $26,600,000 - $14,500,000 = $12,100,000.

math.setup: Adjusted net margin = prior net margin - lost CM from departing business passengers

questions.prompt: Deduct the annual promotion overhead cost to arrive at the final net result.

math.setup: Final net = adjusted net margin - promotion overhead

brainstorming.prompt: What steps could the airline take to minimize the loss of business passengers who are dissatisfied with more children on board?

categories.name: Boarding process
ideas: Separate priority boarding lanes for business travelers
Early boarding for families with children so business passengers board after cabins are settled

categories.name: Seating arrangement
ideas: Seat children and accompanying families in the rear cabin
Create a family section distinct from the business-heavy rows

categories.name: In-flight experience
ideas: Provide noise-canceling headphones to business passengers
Designate quiet zones toward the front of the aircraft

categories.name: Check-in and airport experience
ideas: Dedicated check-in lines for business travelers
Lounge access unaffected by the promotion

recommendation: Implement the promotion: the net financial impact is positive at $9,100,000 per year after all costs, churn adjustments, and promotion overhead
The promotion does not breach capacity (1,390,000 vs. 1,500,000 seats), so there is no operational constraint
risks: 50,000 business passengers defecting due to increased children on board (already modeled, but churn could be higher if estimate is conservative)
Competitive retaliation — other airlines may launch similar or more aggressive promotions, eroding the new customer gain
Consumer habituation — customers may come to expect the promotion, making it difficult to withdraw without a loyalty penalty
Current paying children shifting to free travel representing a permanent revenue loss
next_steps: Implement mitigations to retain business passengers (separate boarding, rear seating for families) before launch
Run a pilot on one route to validate the 150,000 new customer and 50,000 churn assumptions
Monitor competitor response closely in the first two quarters
Establish a sunset or review clause to evaluate continuation after 12 months
